name: Functional Requirement
subject: blockchain
subjectTitle: Blockchain: A Skeptic's Guide to Trust Technologies

lesson.title: From Goals to Specs: Turning a Business Requirement Into Something Buildable
lesson.summary: A functional requirement translates a business requirement's plain-language goal into a precise, testable system behavior, and stating requirements at this level of precision is what lets a team decide honestly which parts of a system, if any, actually need blockchain technology.
lesson.body:
A functional requirement describes a specific behavior a system must perform: what it does, step by step, in response to a given input or action, stated precisely enough that an engineer can build it and someone else can test whether it was built correctly. Where a business requirement, discussed in the previous section, describes an outcome the organization needs in plain, non-technical language, a functional requirement translates that outcome into the concrete capabilities a system must actually have. Taking the earlier example, a business requirement like let any customer independently verify that a product batch passed its safety inspection might translate into several functional requirements: the system must let an inspector record a pass or fail result tied to a specific batch identifier, the system must let anyone look up a batch identifier and see its recorded result, and the system must prevent an already recorded result from being altered after the fact.

This translation step is where a decision about blockchain technology actually gets made responsibly, rather than assumed from the start. Each functional requirement can be evaluated against candidate technologies on its own terms. Prevent an already recorded result from being altered is a functional requirement that a public blockchain satisfies naturally, since a confirmed transaction becomes practically infeasible to rewrite once enough subsequent blocks have been added, a property that traces directly back to the computational cost of doing so. But let anyone look up a batch identifier does not specifically require a blockchain at all, a conventional database with a public application programming interface could satisfy that same functional requirement, often at dramatically lower operating expense and infrastructure cost than an equivalent blockchain-based system, as covered in earlier sections.

This is exactly why separating functional requirements from the technology used to satisfy them matters so much in practice. A team can look at their full list of functional requirements and ask, for each one individually, which possible system actually needs it, and only reach for blockchain technology for the specific requirements that genuinely benefit from its particular properties, tamper resistance, decentralized verification, no single party controlling the record, rather than adopting it wholesale because the project sounds more modern with it. In the batch verification example, a hybrid design often makes the most sense: use a blockchain specifically for the tamper resistance requirement, recording just a compact fingerprint of each inspection result on-chain, while handling ordinary lookups through a conventional, much cheaper database that references those on-chain records when tamper-proof verification is actually needed.

Functional requirements, stated this precisely, also become the basis for the cost analysis that runs through much of this material: transaction cost depends on how many functional requirements actually require writing to the blockchain, operating expense depends on how often those functions get invoked in practice, and infrastructure cost depends on what it takes to keep the system available to satisfy them reliably. A vague business requirement produces vague functional requirements, and vague functional requirements make it nearly impossible to judge honestly, before money is spent, whether blockchain technology was ever the right tool for the job in the first place.
